about_org.heading: About Total Body Therapy & Wellness
about_org.body: Founded in Lillington, NC in 2008 with the goal of bringing exceptional "Big City Care" to a small-town community. Physical therapy in Harnett County since 2002.
points: Whole-person approach — we treat the total body, not just the part
Patient education as a core part of the plan of care

objectives: Describe the structure and function of the lymphatic system
Differentiate primary from secondary lymphedema and identify risk factors
Recognize the symptomatology and clinical presentation of lymphedema
Perform and interpret key diagnostic tests, including Stemmer's sign
Stage lymphedema using ISL criteria, Stage 0 through Stage III
Apply the four components of Complete Decongestive Therapy
Select an appropriate long-term compression garment, including adjustable wrap and custom options
Distinguish lipedema from lymphedema and stage lipedema appropriately
Identify red flags requiring physician referral
Identify gait, balance, and orthopedic needs that persist after decongestion

sections.title: The Lymphatic System
sections.lead: A one-way drainage network running parallel to the venous system, returning fluid, protein, and immune cells to circulation.

items: **Protein transport** — the only route back for large proteins

blocks.detail: Lymphangions are segments that contract 6–10x/min. The left side and the entire lower body drain via the thoracic duct; the right upper quadrant via the right lymphatic duct.

sections.note: Lymphangion contraction is the primary pump. It is stimulated by stretch, muscle contraction, arterial pulsation, and breathing — which is exactly why exercise and diaphragmatic breathing are treatment, not just adjuncts.

sections.title: Lymph Load vs. Transport Capacity
sections.lead: Every case of lymphedema is a mismatch between how much fluid needs to move and how much the system can move.

items: **Dynamic insufficiency** — normal vessels, excess load. Ordinary edema.
**Mechanical insufficiency** — damaged vessels. This is lymphedema.
Retained protein is osmotically active — pulls in water
Fibrosis further cuts capacity — a self-reinforcing loop
blocks.detail: This is why untreated lymphedema progresses, and why early intervention changes the trajectory.

sections.note: Combined insufficiency — high load AND damaged system — is common in the patients you will actually see.

sections.title: Primary vs. Secondary Lymphedema
sections.lead: Primary lymphedema arises from congenital lymphatic dysplasia. Secondary lymphedema follows anatomical disruption of a previously normal system.

items: **Congenital** — birth to age 2, incl. Milroy disease
**Praecox** — puberty to 35. Most common primary form.
blocks.detail: Mechanisms: aplasia, hypoplasia, hyperplasia, or valvular incompetence.

items: **Cancer treatment** — node dissection and/or radiation. Leading cause here.
blocks.detail: Risk multipliers after cancer treatment: extent of node dissection, regional radiation, elevated BMI, post-op infection, wound complications, taxane-based chemo.

sections.note: Risk multipliers after cancer treatment: extent of node dissection, regional radiation, elevated BMI, post-op infection, wound complications, and taxane-based chemotherapy.

sections.title: Symptomatology
sections.lead: Subjective symptoms frequently precede visible swelling by months. Do not wait for a measurable difference to take a patient seriously.

blocks.h: Early — often reported before anything is visible
items: Clothing, rings or shoes fitting differently
Persistent swelling, no longer resolving with elevation
Psychosocial burden — body image, social withdrawal
Functional loss — grip, reach, gait, footwear

sections.note: Lymphedema is typically painless early. New or significant pain suggests infection, DVT, malignancy — or lipedema, which is painful by definition.

sections.title: Diagnosis and Measurement
sections.lead: Diagnosis is primarily clinical. History and physical examination identify the great majority of cases.

items: Onset, duration, whether it resolves overnight
Surgical and oncologic history — nodes, radiation fields
**Stemmer's sign** — cannot lift the skin fold = positive = lymphedema
blocks.detail: Stemmer's is diagnostic when positive; a negative does NOT rule lymphedema out. Check between the toes for tinea — a common cellulitis entry point.

items: **Circumferential tape** at 4 cm intervals — cheap, reliable

blocks.h: Imaging — when the picture is unclear

sections.note: Severity by volume difference vs. the contralateral limb: minimal <20%, moderate 20–40%, severe >40%.

sections.title: What Else Swells a Limb
sections.lead: Before you treat it as lymphedema, rule these out.

rows: Acute unilateral onset, pain, warmth, erythema. URGENT — do not perform MLD.
Hemosiderin staining, varicosities, medial malleolar ulceration, improves with elevation
Bilateral, dependent, pitting, dyspnea, JVD, orthopnea
Bilateral, generalized, may include ascites/periorbital edema
Bilateral, symmetrical, painful, bruises easily, SPARES THE FEET, negative Stemmer
Rapid onset, pain, proximal-first, neurologic signs. Requires imaging.
Fever, spreading erythema, heat, pain. Antibiotics first — MLD contraindicated.
Calcium channel blockers, NSAIDs, steroids, gabapentin, some diabetes drugs

sections.note: Malignant lymphedema and DVT are the two that must not be missed. Both are referrals, not treatment plans.

sections.title: ISL Staging — Overview
sections.lead: The International Society of Lymphology defines four stages. Stage 0 is latent — the lymphatics are already impaired before anything is visible.
sections.note: Staging describes tissue condition, not size. A small Stage III limb is still Stage III. Severity is graded separately by volume difference.

sections.title: Latent / Subclinical
sections.lead: Lymph transport is already impaired. No visible swelling. May persist for months or years before progressing.

items: Subjective heaviness, tightness, or fullness may be reported
Reduced transport capacity detectable by bioimpedance or lymphoscintigraphy
This is the highest-value window for intervention
Baseline measurement pre-operatively makes this stage detectable at all
Surveillance program, risk-reduction education, early compression if indicated
Prophylactic PT after node dissection has been shown to reduce progression

sections.photo_slot: Stage 0 — no visible change; consider a limb-surveillance/measurement photo instead

sections.title: Spontaneously Reversible
sections.lead: Early accumulation of protein-rich fluid. Swelling reduces with elevation — often resolving completely overnight.

items: Subsides with elevation; frequently gone by morning
**No secondary tissue changes** — no fibrosis yet
Limb feels heavy; may be visibly larger by end of day
Compression garments often sufficient for maintenance
Patient education on self-management is decisive here
Goal: prevent the transition to fibrosis

sections.photo_slot: Stage I — soft pitting edema, dorsum of foot or hand

sections.title: Spontaneously Irreversible
sections.lead: Elevation alone no longer reduces the swelling. Lymphostatic fibrosis has begun and the tissue is changing character.

items: **Early Stage II** — pitting is manifest and pronounced
**Late Stage II** — pitting may be absent as fibrosis replaces fluid
Tissue feels firm; **Stemmer's sign becomes positive**
Fibrosis requires manual work plus foam/chip padding under bandaging
Realistic goal is volume reduction and stabilization, not cure

sections.note: The presence or absence of pitting is what separates early from late Stage II — not the size of the limb.
sections.photo_slot: Stage II — firm non-pitting swelling, positive Stemmer, early skin thickening

sections.title: Lymphostatic Elephantiasis
sections.lead: Extreme volume increase with characteristic trophic skin changes. Pitting is typically absent.

items: Marked volume increase and limb distortion
Lymphorrhea — weeping of lymph fluid through the skin
Extended intensive phase; often requires wound care alongside CDT
Meaningful volume reduction is still achievable — do not write these patients off
Coordinate with physician; surgical options may be considered after conservative management

sections.note: Stage III is not a treatment failure to be managed passively. Significant reduction is well documented with sustained CDT.
sections.photo_slot: Stage III — elephantiasis, papillomas, deep skin folds

sections.title: Complete Decongestive Therapy
sections.lead: CDT is the internationally accepted standard of care. It has four components, delivered in two phases.

pillars.d: Reduce bacterial and fungal load; protect the primary infection barrier
Redirect lymph to functioning territories via light, specific manual technique
Counter refilling, soften fibrosis, sustain the reduction achieved
Use the muscle pump under compression to drive lymph transport

items: MLD, multilayer short-stretch bandaging worn 23 hours/day, exercise, skin care
Ends when volume plateaus across consecutive sessions
Fitted compression garment during the day; night garment or bandaging as needed
Ongoing surveillance; garments replaced every 4–6 months
Return for a short intensive phase if the limb regresses

sections.note: Phase II is where outcomes are actually won or lost. Adherence, not technique, is the usual determinant of long-term result.

sections.title: Skin & Nail Care
sections.lead: A lymphedematous limb is immunocompromised tissue. The skin is the last barrier, and every infection causes further lymphatic damage.

items: Wash with low-pH, fragrance-free cleanser — lymphedematous skin is alkaline-shifted
Dry thoroughly, especially **between the toes and in skin folds**
Apply low-pH emollient to keep the barrier intact
Inspect the entire limb daily, including between digits and the posterior surface
Treat tinea pedis and onychomycosis aggressively — a common cellulitis entry point
Nails cut straight across; avoid cutting cuticles
Avoid blood draws, IVs, and BP cuffs on the at-risk limb where an alternative exists
Protect during gardening, cooking, pet handling; gloves and insect repellent
Prompt antiseptic care for any break in the skin

blocks.h: Teach the patient to recognize cellulitis
items: Spreading redness, heat, tenderness, sudden limb enlargement
**Seek care same-day. Stop MLD and compression until treated.**
Recurrent cellulitis may warrant prophylactic antibiotics — physician decision

sections.photo_slot: Skin care — emollient application, interdigital inspection

sections.title: Manual Lymphatic Drainage
sections.lead: A specific, very light manual technique that stimulates lymphangion contraction and redirects lymph across watersheds into functioning territories.

items: Skin moves with the hand — no lubricant, no gliding
blocks.detail: Heavy pressure collapses initial lymphatics and is counterproductive. Order: neck/terminus, then trunk quadrants, then the limb. Work root-to-tip to clear, then tip-to-root to drain.

items: Caution: active malignancy — coordinate with oncology
blocks.detail: Acute renal failure is also a contraindication. Carotid sinus hypersensitivity is a caution for neck work.

sections.note: MLD alone produces modest results. Its value is greatest when combined with compression — the evidence supports CDT as a package, not MLD in isolation.

sections.title: Compression Therapy
sections.lead: The single most important component for maintaining reduction. Without compression, gains from MLD reverse within hours.

items: Foam over fibrosis; gradient higher distally
Flat-knit preferred; custom for irregular shape
Acute DVT, acute infection, severe neuropathy
blocks.detail: Intermittent pneumatic compression is an adjunct only. Never use it over an untreated proximal obstruction.

sections.note: Intermittent pneumatic compression may be a useful adjunct but does not replace MLD or bandaging, and must not be used over an untreated proximal obstruction.
sections.photo_slot: Compression — short-stretch bandaging layers and flat-knit garment

sections.title: Remedial Exercise
sections.lead: The skeletal muscle pump is a primary driver of lymph transport. Exercise performed under compression is decongestive therapy.

items: Diaphragmatic breathing to start and finish
Progressive resistance training does **not** cause or worsen lymphedema
**Do not tell patients to avoid using the limb**
blocks.detail: Progress gradually, wear compression, monitor and stop for symptom change. Advising disuse is outdated and causes deconditioning. Aquatic exercise is especially effective — hydrostatic pressure provides uniform compression while the patient moves.

sections.note: Aquatic exercise is particularly effective — hydrostatic pressure provides uniform external compression while the patient moves.
sections.photo_slot: Exercise — patient exercising in compression garment

sections.title: Long-Term Compression Garments
sections.lead: Phase II is where the result is held. The garment has to fit the limb, the diagnosis, and the patient's hands — a garment that cannot be donned will not be worn.

items: **Knee-high** — most common; easiest to don, best adherence
**Thigh-high** — swelling above the knee; needs a silicone band
**Capri** — thigh and knee, spared calf. Common in lipedema.
Far easier with arthritis, weak grip, or limited reach
Available for calf, foot/ankle, and upper limb
**Flat-knit** — seamed, made to measure, stiffer. Preferred for lymphedema.
**Circular-knit** — thinner, more cosmetic, tourniquets at folds
Any distortion, fibrosis, or deep folds → flat-knit

blocks.h: Custom garments — when off-the-shelf will not do
items: **Compression bras** for trunk and chest wall
Genital, head and neck; 2–3 weeks to fabricate
blocks.detail: Measured by a certified fitter. Jobst and Juzo both produce made-to-measure flat-knit lines.

items: **Two garments** so one is always clean
Replace every 4–6 months — elastic fatigues before it looks worn
Check arterial status first; ABI < 0.8 caution
Donning aids: rubber gloves, donner, slip-sock

sections.note: The most common cause of Phase II failure is not the wrong pressure class — it is a garment the patient cannot physically get on. Assess grip, reach, and vision before prescribing, and reach for an adjustable wrap when donning is the limiting factor.

sections.title: Lipedema — A Different Disease
sections.lead: A chronic disorder of adipose tissue, almost exclusively affecting women, routinely misdiagnosed as obesity or lymphedema for years before recognition.

items: **Painful** — tender to pressure. Diagnostic, not incidental.
blocks.detail: Also: disproportionate — lower body markedly larger than trunk. The affected fat does not respond to caloric restriction or exercise.

items: Evidence points to a connective tissue component
Reported in up to ~11% of women
Patients are told to lose weight — it does not work
Years of shame and ineffective treatment
Delay allows progression to lymphatic involvement

sections.note: Sarah Bramblette and patient advocacy groups have driven recent recognition, but average time to diagnosis remains measured in years.

sections.title: Lipedema Staging
sections.lead: Classically staged 1 through 3 by skin and tissue architecture. A fourth stage — lipo-lymphedema — is widely used clinically but is contested.

items: Enlarged hypodermis; homogeneous thickening of subcutaneous tissue
Fat is often soft; small nodules may be palpable — described as rice-like or pearl-sized
Fat accumulation around pelvis, buttocks, and hips
Limbs tender and prone to bruising
Swelling may improve with rest and elevation
Skin surface becomes bumpy and wave-like with indentations
Nodular structures in the thickened subcutis — lipomas, angiolipomas
Subcutaneous tissue feels tougher and more nodular
Fat build-up extends down the legs toward the ankles
Swelling less responsive to rest and elevation than Stage 1
Symptoms range from mild to severe
Bulky, overhanging extrusions of skin and fat
Marked deformation of thighs and around the knees
Persistent swelling not resolving with rest or elevation
Mobility significantly impaired; highest rate of orthopedic complication
May be associated with secondary lymphedema
Lipedema plus secondary lymphedema in the same limbs
**The feet begin to swell** — the defining change
Skin over the toes thickens; pitting appears
Diagnosis moves from lipedema to lipo-lymphedema
Lymphoscintigraphy can document the degree of drainage impairment

sections.note: IMPORTANT CAVEAT: The Lipedema Foundation no longer uses a 'Stage 4' designation, on the grounds that the lymphatic system can be compromised at any stage — lymphatic impairment is documented in Stages 2 and 3. Present Stage 4 as lipo-lymphedema, and note the debate. This is the intellectually honest framing and it will be the question a sharp student asks.

sections.title: Lipedema vs. Lymphedema
sections.lead: The differential that matters most in practice — and the one most often gotten wrong.

rows: Painless early; tension pain when advanced
Not primarily fat; weight loss reduces risk

sections.note: They co-exist. Lipedema does not itself cause lymphedema — but central obesity, which frequently accompanies it, substantially raises lymphedema risk. Treat what you find.

sections.title: PT Management of Lipedema
sections.lead: Conservative management does not remove lipedema fat. It manages pain, controls fluid, preserves mobility, and slows progression.

items: Pain reduction — often the patient's priority
MLD for fluid and for pain
Conservative care does not remove the fat
Liposuction is the only intervention that does
PT before and after surgery improves outcomes

sections.note: The single most valuable thing you may do is tell the patient this is a recognized disease and not a personal failure of willpower.

sections.title: Other Considerations After Lymphatic PT
sections.lead: Decongestion is not the end of the episode of care. Once volume is controlled, what remains is often what limits the patient most.

items: Gait adapted around a heavy limb persists after decongestion
Reassess step length, cadence, base of support
**Shoe size often changes after Phase I**
Calf pump is both a gait and a lymphatic goal
blocks.detail: Address compensations: circumduction, hip hiking, reduced push-off.

items: Altered limb mass and distal sensation degrade postural control
**Screen falls risk** — rarely done in this population
Proprioceptive retraining at ankle and hip
A fall breaking skin is a cellulitis risk
blocks.detail: Compounding factors: chemotherapy-induced peripheral neuropathy, deconditioning, visual change.

blocks.h: Orthopedic pain not relieved by CDT
items: If pain persists once volume is controlled, treat it as a separate problem
Knee and hip OA; low back pain from gait asymmetry
Re-measure at regular intervals; catch regression early
Short repeat intensive phase if the limb regresses — this is expected, not failure
Re-screen falls risk and function, not just limb volume

sections.note: Patients are frequently discharged the moment limb volume plateaus. The gait, balance, and orthopedic findings underneath are what determine whether they actually return to their life — and they are squarely within PT scope.

sections.title: Red Flags & Referral
sections.lead: Stop treatment and refer when you see these.

items: **Suspected DVT** — acute unilateral swelling, calf pain
Rapid-onset or proximal-first swelling — possible malignancy
Failure to respond to well-delivered CDT

sections.note: MLD is contraindicated in acute infection, acute DVT, and decompensated heart failure. When in doubt, do not treat — refer.

sections.title: Key Takeaways
numbered: Lymphedema is mechanical insufficiency — high-protein, progressive, and self-reinforcing if untreated.
Symptoms precede visible swelling. Stage 0 is real and is the best time to intervene.
Stemmer's sign is fast, free, and diagnostic when positive.
Four ISL stages: 0 latent, I reversible, II irreversible/fibrotic, III elephantiasis.
CDT has four components. Compression is the one that holds the result.
Exercise under compression is treatment. Resistance training is safe.
Garment choice is decided as much by whether the patient can don it as by pressure class.
Lipedema is painful, symmetrical, spares the feet, and has a negative Stemmer.
Lipedema is staged 1–3, with lipo-lymphedema as a contested Stage 4.
Every episode of cellulitis makes the underlying disease worse.
Patient education and Phase II adherence determine long-term outcome.
Decongestion is not discharge — reassess gait, balance, and orthopedic pain afterwards.

quiz.q: A patient reports her arm feels heavy and her rings are tight, but you can see no swelling and measurements match the other side. What ISL stage is this, and does it need treatment?
quiz.a: Stage 0 — latent/subclinical. Lymph transport is already impaired even though nothing is visible. Yes, it needs attention: this is the highest-value window for intervention. Start surveillance, risk-reduction education, and consider early compression.

quiz.q: You attempt to pinch the skin at the base of the second toe and cannot lift a fold. What is this sign, and what does it tell you?
quiz.a: A positive Stemmer's sign. It is diagnostic for lymphedema. Note the asymmetry of the test: a positive result confirms lymphedema, but a negative result does NOT rule it out.

quiz.q: What single finding most reliably separates early Stage II from late Stage II?
quiz.a: Whether the tissue pits. Early Stage II shows manifest pitting; in late Stage II pitting may be absent as lymphostatic fibrosis replaces fluid. Limb size does not determine the stage.

quiz.q: Why is heavy pressure wrong during manual lymphatic drainage?
quiz.a: Initial lymphatics are blind-ended, thin-walled vessels anchored by filaments. Heavy pressure collapses them, blocking uptake. MLD uses pressure light enough only to stretch the skin, at roughly one stroke per second to match lymphangion contraction rate.

quiz.q: Why must you clear proximal territories before working distally?
quiz.a: Fluid has to have somewhere to go. If the trunk quadrant and terminus are still congested, mobilizing distal fluid simply pushes it into a full receiving area. Always empty the receiving territory first.

quiz.q: Why short-stretch and never long-stretch (ACE) bandages?
quiz.a: Short-stretch gives low resting pressure and high working pressure — it resists the muscle during contraction but does not constrict at rest. Long-stretch has high resting pressure and can act as a tourniquet over the 23 hours a day the bandage is worn.

quiz.q: A patient with lower-limb lymphedema has an ABI of 0.6. What do you do?
quiz.a: Do not apply standard compression. ABI below 0.8 requires caution and below 0.5 is a contraindication. Arterial insufficiency means compression can compromise perfusion. Refer for vascular assessment and coordinate on modified or reduced compression.

quiz.q: A breast cancer survivor with Stage I arm lymphedema asks whether she should stop lifting weights. What is the evidence-based answer?
quiz.a: No. Slowly progressive resistance training does not cause or worsen lymphedema, and the PAL trial demonstrated safety in this exact population. It may reduce flares. Progress gradually, wear compression during exercise, and monitor for symptom change. Advising limb disuse is outdated and causes deconditioning.

quiz.q: Bilateral symmetrical leg swelling, painful and tender, bruises easily, stops abruptly at the ankles with normal-looking feet, negative Stemmer. Diagnosis?
quiz.a: Lipedema. The combination of pain, symmetry, easy bruising, foot-sparing with a sharp ankle cuff, and a negative Stemmer's sign distinguishes it from lymphedema.

quiz.q: That same patient returns two years later. Her feet are now swelling, Stemmer is positive, and the skin over her toes has thickened. What changed?
quiz.a: She has developed lipo-lymphedema — secondary lymphedema on top of her lipedema, commonly called Stage 4. Foot involvement and a positive Stemmer are the defining transition. Note that the Lipedema Foundation no longer uses the Stage 4 label, since lymphatic compromise can occur at any stage.

quiz.q: Name the three absolute contraindications to MLD.
quiz.a: Acute cellulitis or active infection, acute DVT, and decompensated congestive heart failure. Acute renal failure is also a contraindication, and active untreated malignancy requires coordination with oncology.

quiz.q: A patient in Phase II calls: her leg is suddenly larger, hot, red, and she feels feverish. What do you tell her?
quiz.a: Seek medical care the same day — this is likely cellulitis. Stop MLD and compression until it is treated. Every episode causes further lymphatic damage, so recurrent cellulitis may warrant prophylactic antibiotics, which is a physician decision.

capabilities.lead: This site is a static presentation platform. Here is what it can do now, what can be added, and what the trade-offs are.

items: Present live from a phone, tablet, or laptop; audience follows along on their own device.
Self-check questions that stay hidden until tapped. Runs entirely in the visitor's browser.
Scannable from the back of a room. Points audience straight to the presentation.
Separate scannable agenda so viewers can jump to a section.
Each lives in its own subdirectory. The homepage lists them automatically.
Built and tested at phone width first.
Any page prints cleanly from the browser.
Edit content, rebuild, push — live in under a minute.

groups.h: Can be added — no backend, no cost
items: Drag between two stages to see the progression.
Type a term, get the definition.
Remembers which sections a visitor has read, on their device only.
Timed or scored version with a results summary.
PDF patient-education sheets linked from any section.
Technique demonstrations hosted on YouTube or Vimeo.
A presenter-only page with prompts, hidden from the public URL.

groups.h: Needs a form service — free tiers available
items: Audience types a question during the talk; it goes privately to the presenter's inbox. Nothing displays publicly.
Collects attendee name and email for records.
groups.note: Options: Web3Forms (up to 250 submissions/month free, no account needed), Basin (100/month free), or an embedded Google Form. All are host-independent and keep working if the site moves.

items: Visitors would post personal health details — their surgeries, their limbs — publicly under the practice name, with no moderation queue and no way to retract. Use the private question box instead.
Creates an expectation of clinical advice outside a documented patient relationship.
Identifiable health information on a public static host. Not appropriate without a HIPAA-compliant system.
Storing any patient data on this site
A static site has no secure storage. Anything genuinely confidential belongs in the clinic's EMR.
GitHub Pages — free, unlimited bandwidth for this scale, requires the repository to be public.
GitHub Pages serves files. It cannot run server code, so anything storing data needs an outside service.

Netlify's free plan is 300 credits/month with production deploys at 15 credits each — roughly 20 deploys before the cap. Form submissions are now free and unlimited on credit plans. Free accounts cannot auto-recharge, so the cap is hard.
Stay on GitHub Pages for hosting. Add a third-party form endpoint if interactive input is wanted. This avoids the deploy-credit ceiling entirely.
